notes.meaning: God led Israel out of Egypt, delivering them from a kingdom whose speech and culture were foreign to them. Even though they lived in Egypt for centuries, it was never their true home, and the language barrier added to their feeling of exile. This departure marked the birth of Israel as a free nation under God's care.

When God brought Israel out of slavery, the people became His holy dwelling place and His royal kingdom. The names Judah and Israel are paired to show that God claimed all twelve tribes as His own possession. Rather than living in a physical building alone, the Lord chose to dwell among His redeemed people and rule over them.

The Red Sea parted when Israel left Egypt, and forty years later the Jordan River stopped flowing so they could enter the Promised Land. The poet speaks of these waters as if they saw God coming and ran away in fear. Putting the two miracles side by side reminds us that the God who began their journey was faithful to bring them all the way home.

Mount Sinai and the hills around it shook violently when God came down to give His Law to Moses. The quaking earth is described poetically, like rams and little lambs leaping and skipping about. Even the heaviest and oldest mountains tremble when their Creator draws near.

The writer directly questions the Red Sea and the Jordan River, asking why they fled and turned backward. Water normally flows according to fixed natural laws, so reversing course was completely extraordinary. This dramatic question builds excitement by making the reader pause and wonder what great power caused such a reaction.

The questioning continues toward the great mountains and rolling hills, asking why they leaped like sheep. Solid rock and ancient peaks cannot move on their own, yet they shook as if panic had struck them. These questions highlight how unnatural it is for mountains to dance unless something truly astonishing has happened.

The psalm now answers the questions of the previous verses by commanding the whole earth to tremble before the Lord. God had not been named until this point, creating suspense before revealing that His arrival caused all this upheaval. The One who shook nature is both the Master of creation and the faithful covenant God of Jacob.

The song closes by recalling how God brought streams of fresh water out of hard flint rock to save His thirsty people in the desert. His great power was not used only to split seas and shake mountains, but to show tender, practical care for Israel's daily needs. God can bring life and refreshing from the hardest and most unlikely places in our lives.
